item.title: Zep Temporal Memory and Stale Facts: A Reproducible 30-Case Fixture (2026)
item.description: A 30-case, stdlib-only fixture that separates stale facts caused by a store's invalidation policy from stale facts caused by extraction error, with the full 16-cell result matrix.
item.content:encoded:
An agent answers “your plan is the Starter tier” three weeks after the account moved to Enterprise. The fact is in the store. The store has timestamps. The answer is still wrong. When that happens the team usually has three suspects and no way to tell them apart: the extraction step filed something incorrectly, the store’s invalidation rule never closed the old fact, or the retrieval query asked the wrong question. This post is a fixture that splits those three apart on paper and in code, so you can tell which one you are looking at. To be precise about the scope: what the fixture exercises is four modelled invalidation policies, not Zep or Graphiti themselves — neither product is run anywhere below. The governance version of the same argument is in the anatomy of persistent memory; this post is the measurement that argument does not carry.

What Zep and Graphiti actually claim about temporal invalidation

The primary source is arXiv:2501.13956, “Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory”, submitted 2025-01-20 by Rasmussen, Paliychuk, Beauvais, Ryan and Chalef. All five authors are Zep-affiliated, and as of 2026-10-30 the arXiv API lists a single version, v1. The abstract reports Deep Memory Retrieval accuracy of 94.8% against 93.4% for MemGPT, and LongMemEval accuracy improvements of up to 18.5% with a 90% latency reduction against “baseline implementations”. Those are vendor-authored claims. This post does not re-run them, and nothing below should be read as a check on them.

The framework documentation is more specific about the mechanism. The Graphiti README states that facts “have validity windows”, that “when information changes, old facts are invalidated — not deleted”, and that a caller can “query what’s true now, or what was true at any point in time”. Its comparison table contrasts “explicit bi-temporal tracking with automatic fact invalidation” against “basic timestamp tracking”. The Graphiti docs overview describes the framework as covering “entity and edge extraction, the bi-temporal model, fact invalidation, and hybrid retrieval”, and says edges “include temporal metadata to record relationship lifecycles”. Repository metadata re-read on 2026-11-24 from the GitHub REST API shows Apache-2.0, 33,049 stars, last push 2026-11-24T00:19:58Z, and the latest release tagged mcp-v1.1.4 published 2026-11-23T21:44:16Z; the 2026-10-30 read recorded 32,367 stars with v0.31.2. Metadata only: no Graphiti process, graph database or LLM extraction call was made for this article.

That distinction matters because documentation describes a design contract, not observed behaviour. If the paper’s pages go deeper on what those benchmarks measure, the source-based review of Zep’s paper covers it; this page deliberately does not re-litigate it.

Why vendor benchmarks cannot answer the stale-fact question

DMR and LongMemEval score end-task answers. Neither reports a stale-return rate, and neither separates an error caused by the store’s invalidation rule from an error caused by a fact that was never extracted correctly in the first place. A model that answers a temporal question well can still be reading a superseded edge; a model that answers badly may simply have been handed the wrong fact. The paper and the framework documentation, as of 2026-10-30, do not publish a measurement that isolates the two — which is not the same as claiming nobody has measured it, only that these four artifacts do not.

So the useful question for a team is narrower than “is this memory layer accurate”: given the same 30 changing facts, does the invalidation policy change how often a superseded value comes back, and how much of the residual error is extraction?

The fixture: 30 cases, four policies, two instants, two extraction arms

The fixture is scripts/stale_fact_fixture.py — Python standard library only, no network at run time, no model, no container. Its input is a frozen dataset of 30 scripted facts, fixtures/stale_fact_cases.json: each case names an entity, an attribute, and two or three events carrying a value, a valid-time window and an ingestion timestamp. The fixture validates that each case’s windows are disjoint and that at most one event covers each evaluation instant — with deliberate zero-coverage instants where the truthful answer is “no active fact” (20 of the 60 case-instant pairs: the ten late-arriving corrections fall into a gap between windows at 2026-08-01, and the ten time-bounded cases have nothing valid left at 2026-10-29) — so the correct answer at any moment is known by construction rather than by judgement.

The cases cover three change shapes. Ten are in-order updates, where ingestion order agrees with valid-time order. Ten are late-arriving corrections, where a fact for a historical window is ingested after the current value, so the most recently ingested edge is not the current truth. Ten are time-bounded validity, where the attribute simply lapsed, so the truthful current answer is “no active fact”.

Four store policies are implemented in roughly fifteen lines each, as stand-ins for design patterns rather than for any product: append-only with recency ranking, last-write-wins upsert, bitemporal invalidation (supersession stamped from valid-time order, an edge closed at its successor’s valid_from), and bitemporal invalidation plus a query-time as-of predicate. Each policy is evaluated at two instants — “what is X now” at 2026-10-29 and “what was X on 2026-08-01” — and under two extraction conditions: a clean store, and a seeded arm in which 3 of 30 cases (10%) have the edge covering the current instant stored under a wrong attribute, modelling a mis-extraction.

An error is counted as extraction-attributable only when that same policy answered the same case correctly with a clean store. If the policy was already wrong with a perfect store, the error stays with the policy. That rule is what keeps the attribution from flattering either side.

Results: the full 16-cell matrix

Run with python3 research/evidence/zep-temporal-memory-stale-fact-fixture-2026/scripts/stale_fact_fixture.py. The published output is results/stale_fact_matrix.csv, reproduced here row for row:

policy query arm n exact correct exact accuracy stale returns stale rate extraction errors policy errors
append_only_recency current clean 30 10 33.3 20 66.7 0 20
append_only_recency current mis_extraction_10pct 30 9 30.0 21 70.0 1 20
append_only_recency as_of clean 30 14 46.7 16 53.3 0 16
append_only_recency as_of mis_extraction_10pct 30 15 50.0 15 50.0 0 15
lww_upsert current clean 30 10 33.3 20 66.7 0 20
lww_upsert current mis_extraction_10pct 30 9 30.0 21 70.0 1 20
lww_upsert as_of clean 30 14 46.7 16 53.3 0 16
lww_upsert as_of mis_extraction_10pct 30 15 50.0 15 50.0 0 15
bitemporal_invalidate current clean 30 30 100.0 0 0.0 0 0
bitemporal_invalidate current mis_extraction_10pct 30 27 90.0 0 0.0 3 0
bitemporal_invalidate as_of clean 30 4 13.3 16 53.3 0 26
bitemporal_invalidate as_of mis_extraction_10pct 30 6 20.0 13 43.3 0 24
bitemporal_asof current clean 30 30 100.0 0 0.0 0 0
bitemporal_asof current mis_extraction_10pct 30 27 90.0 0 0.0 3 0
bitemporal_asof as_of clean 30 30 100.0 0 0.0 0 0
bitemporal_asof as_of mis_extraction_10pct 30 30 100.0 0 0.0 0 0

Rates are percentages of the 30 evaluations in that cell; “stale returns” counts answers that named a real value of that attribute which was not the value asked for, as opposed to returning no fact at all. The run record is first-party-fixture-run-2026-10-30.json: Python 3.12.3 on Linux aarch64, 2 CPUs, 480 evaluations, and 0.0042 s inside the evaluation loop, which is the only timing the script itself records. Whole-script wall time sits next to it in the same record as an external measurement rather than a script figure: five runs of the script, timed from interpreter start to exit on the same 2-vCPU host, gave 0.056-0.057 s, median 0.057 s. Sub-0.1 s numbers move with host and load — independent re-measurement during review gave 0.07 s for the same script, and a 2026-11-24 relocation check recorded 0.0051 s inside the loop and 0.07 s wall — so read both as “well under a second”, not as a benchmark. No product, model or graph database was executed. When these files moved into the evidence bundle, that check also re-derived the CSV byte for byte and confirmed a tampered copy still fails verification; its verification record carries the current file hashes.

Reading the matrix: policy failure versus extraction failure

Change only the policy, keep extraction clean, and the current-truth question separates hard: append-only recency and last-write-wins both land at 33.3% exact accuracy with a 66.7% stale-return rate, while both bitemporal policies reach 100% with zero stale returns. All twenty clean-arm errors for the recency policies are policy-attributable, and they cluster exactly where you would expect: the ten late-arriving corrections, whose newest-ingested edge is a historical one, and the ten lapsed attributes, whose last ingested edge is expired.

Append-only and last-write-wins produce identical rows in every cell, and that is a finding rather than a bug in the fixture: when retrieval ranks by ingestion time and no temporal predicate is applied, keeping every historical edge and overwriting it are behaviourally the same answer. History that is stored but never queried does not protect anyone.

Change only the query instant and the picture inverts. Without a query-time as-of predicate, the bitemporal policy answers every as-of question with the current truth and scores 13.3% — it only succeeds on the four cases whose value had already stopped changing before 2026-08-01. Adding the predicate takes the same store to 100%. Invalidation alone fixes “what is X now”; it does not give you “what was X then”, which needs the predicate at query time, not at write time.

The 10% extraction arm is where the attribution earns its keep. Under both bitemporal policies, 3 of 30 current-truth answers become wrong and all three are extraction-attributable — the store is right, the fact was filed under the wrong attribute, and the query returns no current fact at all, so the stale-return rate stays at zero while exact accuracy drops to 90%. Mis-extraction under a bitemporal store shows up as silence, not as a stale value. Under the recency policies the same corruption surfaces differently: one case flips to a stale answer, because dropping the newest edge from the ranking promotes the previous one.

Two honest artifacts are worth naming. First, the 10% arm moves the recency policy’s as-of score up, from 46.7% to 50.0%, and the bitemporal policy’s as-of score from 13.3% to 20.0%: removing a fact can accidentally improve a coarse policy, which is exactly why single-cell deltas should not be read as quality signals. Second, the extraction arm’s three faults are a seeded synthetic condition, not a measured extraction error rate of any product.

What this means operationally is narrow but useful. Instrument the two failure modes separately: log the edges your store considers currently valid for an attribute, and log whether the queried attribute had zero current edges. A zero-edge result under a bitemporal store points at extraction or entity resolution; a non-zero edge set containing a superseded value points at the policy or at a write path that never stamped supersession. One counter per failure mode will tell you which one you are paying for.

Reproduce it and check the numbers

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io
cd baeseokjae.github.io
python3 research/evidence/zep-temporal-memory-stale-fact-fixture-2026/scripts/stale_fact_fixture.py --verify

--verify re-derives all sixteen cells from the frozen case file and compares them byte for byte against the published CSV, exiting non-zero on any mismatch; the CSV sha256 recorded here is c1d96ab3fe5b0112e6705f0f22ffa936ce4927517c58b06b4f19da97f9953548. If you edit a policy or add cases, drop --verify to regenerate, then read results/STALE-FACT-NOTES.md for the exact commands, hashes and the two artifacts above. The script, case file, CSV and notes all live in research/evidence/zep-temporal-memory-stale-fact-fixture-2026/, so they stay together and the command works from any checkout. The script and dataset are first-party originals written for this post; no third-party source downloads and no credentials are included.

What this fixture does not prove

It does not test Graphiti or Zep Cloud. No server was installed, no Neo4j, FalkorDB or Neptune instance was created, no extraction model was called, and no account was used. The four policies model documented patterns; the numbers describe those models and nothing about vendor runtime behaviour, latency or cost.

It is synthetic by construction: 30 cases with clean, disjoint valid-time windows and a single attribute per case. Real corpora bring overlapping assertions, entity-resolution ambiguity and extraction quality that no seeded 10% arm represents. Its value is as a control: if a policy cannot suppress superseded facts here, it will not do so on messy data either.

For choosing between vendor memory layers, the Mem0-versus-Zep production guide covers pricing and deployment questions this post does not touch, and the agent memory comparison is the framework selection matrix. If you want to run the equivalent split against a real system rather than a model of one, that is the measurement still missing from this site — and from the sources cited above.

item.title: Zep AI Review 2026: Temporal Knowledge Graphs for Agent Memory
item.description: A source-based review of Zep and Graphiti: temporal memory, correctly scoped benchmark evidence, current pricing, and production evaluation questions.
item.content:encoded:
Zep provides a managed context layer for AI applications, using temporal graph artifacts derived with Graphiti. Graphiti is its open-source temporal knowledge graph framework. This review explains the architecture and its evaluation limits; it does not report an independently reproduced product benchmark. Source: Zep documentation.

Correction — October 7, 2026: The previous version described unrelated benchmark values as an independent Zep-versus-Mem0 comparison and called an arXiv paper peer-reviewed without evidence for that status. Those claims, unverified latency promises and unsupported integration examples have been withdrawn.

What Temporal Memory Adds

A temporal graph represents entities, relationships and the times associated with facts. Graphiti supports ingestion of structured and unstructured information and retrieval that combines semantic, text and graph approaches. Its temporal model can represent changes while preserving historical context. Source: Graphiti overview.

Consider an assistant that first learns that Alice works for one employer and later receives an update naming a different employer. A useful memory system must preserve the evidence, resolve the update and answer both “where does Alice work now?” and “where did Alice work last year?” appropriately.

Temporal metadata helps express that problem. It does not guarantee correct extraction, entity resolution or answers. A missing invalidation timestamp is not proof that a claim is true: the system may not have seen an update, or extraction may have failed. Validate the returned evidence before taking consequential action.

Graph Memory, Vector Retrieval and Full Context

These are implementation choices that can be combined. Vector retrieval can include timestamps, metadata filters, reranking and application-level update rules. It is inaccurate to say that it inherently cannot handle current facts or multi-step retrieval. A graph can make relationships explicit while still relying on embeddings and an LLM.

Approach What to evaluate Common implementation questions
Temporal graph Relationship extraction and time-aware retrieval Wrong merges, missed updates, provenance and deletion
Vector-based retrieval Relevant evidence under filters and ranking rules Duplicate chunks, stale results, chunking and metadata quality
Full conversation context Answer quality using retained source material Input size, latency, cost and irrelevant history

This table describes evaluation concerns, not measured product rankings. Compare systems using the same data, question set, answer model and resource limits before choosing one.

What the Zep Paper Actually Measures

The authors’ January 2025 Zep paper reports the following LongMemEval_s results in Table 2:

Memory method Answer model Reported score
Full context GPT-4o-mini 55.4%
Zep GPT-4o-mini 63.8%
Full context GPT-4o 60.2%
Zep GPT-4o 71.2%

The same table does not contain a Mem0 row. The former “63.8% versus 49.0%, a 15-point advantage” statement therefore does not follow from this experiment. The paper’s authors are associated with Zep; this is author-reported research, not an independent reproduction by this blog. An arXiv posting alone does not establish peer review.

Benchmark results apply to the documented setup and release, not automatically to the current managed service or a self-hosted installation. Model choice, ingestion, retrieval budget, prompts and grading can change the outcome. This article does not assert a current cross-product winner or a universal p99 latency guarantee.

A Fair Memory Evaluation

Use a fixed dataset and question set, including updates, contradictions, deletions and out-of-scope questions. Keep the answer model and scoring procedure the same. Record default settings separately from tuned configurations, and retain the retrieved evidence for each answer.

Measure ingestion cost and latency as well as retrieval and answer generation. Include failure recovery and document what happens when a write succeeds but extraction is delayed or fails. For multi-tenant applications, test whether one user’s data can be retrieved by another. A benchmark accuracy score does not establish that access controls work.

Update, contradiction and delete behaviour is the part of that evaluation teams usually improvise. The agent memory write-path reliability protocol turns it into a runnable check: a fixed write dataset, an adapter contract you implement against the system under test, and scored measures for stale values, flagged contradictions and deletes that actually remove a fact. Treat it as a method to run on your own data, not as a result about any vendor.

Zep Cloud and Graphiti Are Different Deployment Choices

The current documentation distinguishes the Graphiti framework from Zep’s managed context service. Self-hosting the framework requires operating the selected graph storage and model/embedding dependencies. It is not a turnkey duplicate of every managed-service capability.

For current installation and supported configurations, use the Graphiti repository. Pin the version, review its license and follow the corresponding examples. A self-hosted graph can still use a hosted LLM or embedding service, so document the complete data path when local operation matters.

Integration Example Boundaries

The earlier article included guessed wrapper classes and an unsupported memory_type="perpetual" configuration. Those snippets have been removed. Graphiti’s current public API uses methods such as add_episode and search, with explicit episode metadata and asynchronous calls; use the maintained Neo4j quickstart for runnable setup instructions.

If integrating with an agent framework, separate storing context from checkpointing execution state. Decide what is written, which namespace is searched, how errors are handled and what the agent is allowed to reveal. Similar names in an older integration package do not guarantee compatibility with a current SDK.

Pricing: Checked October 20, 2026

Zep’s pricing page currently lists the following monthly self-serve plans:

Plan Monthly price Included credits Additional credits
Flex $125 50,000 $25 per 10,000
Flex Plus $375 200,000 $75 per 40,000
Enterprise Negotiated Negotiated Negotiated

The page offers 10,000 monthly credits for prototyping, subject to limits. It meters episode ingestion by size: one credit for up to 350 bytes, with another credit for each additional 350 bytes or part. Other operations can have different treatment. Check the current limits, billing mode and top-up behavior before budgeting; the earlier 1,000-credit free-tier description was out of date.

For example, a 700-byte episode is two ingestion credits under that rule. This is arithmetic based on the published unit, not a measured workload bill. Determine actual encoded episode sizes and operation counts before projecting spend. See the pricing page’s credit definitions.

Production Questions Before Adoption

Test whether the system answers your domain’s update and relationship questions better than your existing baseline, then examine the operational tradeoffs. Important questions include:

  • Can a user inspect and correct a stored fact and its provenance?
  • What is deleted when an episode, user or graph is removed, and when does deletion take effect?
  • How are namespaces and permissions enforced during retrieval?
  • How are delayed ingestion, retries and inconsistent updates surfaced?
  • What data reaches model providers, and what contractual deployment terms apply?

For regulated workloads, verify the applicable contract, plan and deployment configuration. A vendor’s listed security offering is not blanket approval for every healthcare or financial use. Avoid treating a framework selection as a substitute for those checks.

Alternatives and Selection Criteria

Evaluate alternatives such as Mem0, LangMem, Letta or another retrieval stack against the same requirements rather than carrying forward this article’s previous unsupported scores or fixed price comparisons. Determine whether the real need is durable user facts, document retrieval, execution checkpoints or a combination.

Choose a small representative scenario and compare correctness, evidence quality, integration work, operational cost and failure handling. A more elaborate graph is not automatically better for a small history; a simple baseline that meets the requirements can be the right result of an evaluation.

FAQ

Has this review established that Zep beats Mem0 by 15 points?

No. The cited paper compares Zep with full-context baselines using specified answer models. It does not support the earlier direct Mem0 comparison.

Is the architecture guaranteed to return the current truth?

No. Temporal records can represent updates, but extraction errors, missing evidence and delayed ingestion still require testing and correction.

Is Graphiti the same product as Zep Cloud?

No. The framework and the managed service have different operational responsibilities and capabilities. Check the current documentation for the deployment you intend to use.

Is this a hands-on review with a tested rating?

No. It is a documentation and research review. The earlier numeric rating has been removed because no reproducible scoring rubric or first-party product evaluation supported it.
